new mexico.rufada_status: Yes. New Mexico adopted the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act in 2017 (Senate Bill 60, Laws 2017, chapter 72), effective January 1, 2018. It is codified at NMSA 1978, Sections 46-13-1 through 46-13-18.
new mexico.custodian_access: A fiduciary can get a catalogue of electronic communications (who sent and received messages, and when) and other digital assets such as photos and files, by giving the custodian a written request, a certified death certificate, letters testamentary or of administration, the account identifier, and evidence linking the account to the user. The content of emails and other private messages is disclosed only if the user consented or a court orders it. The custodian must comply within 60 days of receiving the required proof, may grant full or partial access or provide a copy, and may charge a reasonable administrative fee.
new mexico.user_direction: The user can direct disclosure through the custodian's online tool, such as Google Inactive Account Manager or Apple Legacy Contact, or in a will, trust, or power of attorney. The online tool controls first; if there is no online-tool direction, the will, trust, or power of attorney controls; if there is no direction at all, the custodian's terms of service control.
new mexico.terms_of_service: The terms of service cannot override a direction the user gave through an online tool or in a will, trust, or power of attorney. If the user left no direction, the terms of service can limit or eliminate the fiduciary's access.
new mexico.platform_tools: Google Inactive Account Manager lets the user name a trusted contact and choose whether the account is shared or deleted after inactivity. Apple Legacy Contact lets a named person request access to the user's Apple data with a death certificate and an access key. Meta lets a Facebook user name a legacy contact to manage a memorialized account, and Instagram memorializes accounts on request with proof of death. A court order is usually needed for the content of messages.
new mexico.what_to_do: 1. Make an inventory of the person's accounts, devices, and passwords. 2. Check whether the person named anyone through an online tool such as Google Inactive Account Manager or Apple Legacy Contact. 3. Gather the will, trust, or power of attorney and the death certificate. 4. Send each custodian a written request with the death certificate and proof of appointment as personal representative. 5. If the custodian refuses or the content of messages is needed, ask the probate court for an order.
new mexico.state_statute: NMSA 1978, Sections 46-13-1 through 46-13-18 (Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act).
new mexico.agency_name: New Mexico Department of Justice, Consumer Protection Bureau
new mexico.state_note: The act applies to wills and powers of attorney executed, and deaths occurring, before, on, or after July 1, 2017, so even an old will can authorize digital-asset access.
sources: New Mexico Legislature, Senate Bill 60 (2017), enacting the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act
NMSA 1978, Chapter 46, Article 13, Sections 46-13-1 through 46-13-18

oklahoma.rufada_status: No. Oklahoma has NOT adopted RUFADAA. Two independent sources confirm this: ProbatePedia's 2026 state-by-state table lists Oklahoma among the three states that have not adopted RUFADAA, and Law Commentary, citing the National Conference of State Legislatures, likewise names Oklahoma as a holdout, noting a RUFADAA bill has sat in the House Rules Committee since February 2020. The only state law is a narrow 2010 statute, Okla. Stat. tit. 58, Section 269, letting an executor or administrator take control of a deceased person's social networking, microblogging, and email accounts.
oklahoma.custodian_access: There is no Oklahoma statute setting out the RUFADAA catalogue-versus-content rules or a 60-day deadline. Under the 2010 law, an executor or administrator may take control of, continue, or terminate the decedent's social networking, microblogging, and email accounts where otherwise authorized. For anything beyond that, access depends on the custodian's own policies, the user's own directions, and general probate law, and a court order is the usual fallback when a custodian refuses.
oklahoma.user_direction: Because Oklahoma has no RUFADAA priority ladder, there is no state-law rule that an online tool beats a will or that a will beats the terms of service. In practice, the platform's own tools still matter most: Google Inactive Account Manager, Apple Legacy Contact, and Meta's legacy contact let the user name someone in advance, and a will or power of attorney that expressly grants digital-asset authority strengthens the fiduciary's request to the custodian.
oklahoma.terms_of_service: Without RUFADAA, the custodian's terms of service carry much more weight in Oklahoma than in the other states in this batch. If the user left no direction, the terms of service and the custodian's deceased-user policy generally decide what, if anything, the family can get, unless a court orders disclosure.
oklahoma.platform_tools: Google Inactive Account Manager lets the user name a trusted contact and choose whether the account is shared or deleted after inactivity. Apple Legacy Contact lets a named person request access to the user's Apple data with a death certificate and an access key. Meta lets a Facebook user name a legacy contact to manage a memorialized account, and Instagram memorializes accounts on request with proof of death. Because Oklahoma has no RUFADAA, these platform tools are the most reliable way to arrange access in advance.
oklahoma.what_to_do: 1. Make an inventory of the person's accounts, devices, and passwords. 2. Check whether the person named anyone through an online tool such as Google Inactive Account Manager or Apple Legacy Contact. 3. Gather the will and the death certificate, and get appointed as executor or administrator. 4. Contact each custodian with the death certificate and proof of appointment, citing the 2010 statute for social media and email accounts. 5. If the custodian refuses, ask the district court for an order, and expect the process to be slower and less certain than in RUFADAA states.
oklahoma.state_statute: Okla. Stat. tit. 58, Section 269 (2010, House Bill 2800) — executor or administrator control of social networking, microblogging, and email accounts. No RUFADAA statute exists in Oklahoma.
oklahoma.agency_name: Oklahoma Attorney General, Consumer Protection Unit
oklahoma.state_note: Oklahoma is one of only three states that have never adopted RUFADAA, and its only digital-assets law dates to 2010, before smartphones and cloud storage were common, so it covers social media and email but says nothing about photos, crypto, or other digital property.
